tldr: To bridge the execution gap between motion tokens generated by humanoid VLAs and physical whole-body controllers, the authors propose a differentiable training framework that backpropagates physical execution loss gradients directly into the VLA action head via a learned world model. Across four simulation tasks, the average task success rate improved by 12.5 percentage points, and closed-loop operation was demonstrated on a real humanoid.
hero_caption: Overall architecture of DiffGR00T. During training only, the non-differentiable physics simulator is replaced with a learned world model. Body execution losses are backpropagated through the world model, the frozen SONIC decoder, and a 4-step Flow-Matching sampler directly into the VLA action head.
overview:
In recent years, Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models integrating vision, language, and action have achieved remarkable results in robot manipulation. However, extending these models to humanoid whole-body control hits the strict physical barriers of dynamic balance and full-body coordination. In today's prevailing hierarchical approaches, the VLA outputs high-level motion intent (such as latent tokens), and a pretrained whole-body controller translates them into joint commands for tracking. The problem is that tracking errors and tipping risks—the actual physical execution errors—provide no direct feedback to optimize the VLA generator.

To address this, the authors developed DiffGR00T, which inserts a learned, differentiable world model as a proxy for the simulator. By mimicking the robot's forward dynamics with a neural network, it calculates the body's tracking errors and drifts several steps ahead, passing those gradients directly back through the whole-body controller and the Flow-Matching sampling process into the VLA action head (LoRA).

Evaluated on four tasks in the HumanoidArena benchmark, DiffGR00T boosted the average task success rate by 12.5 percentage points over the supervised base VLA, going from 59.2% to 71.7%. Moreover, the number of steps required to achieve success dropped by 20%, and closed-loop execution was achieved on a physical Unitree G1 robot.
contributions: Built an action-conditioned world model that accurately and differentiably approximates the 29-DoF whole-body dynamics of a humanoid.

Established an end-to-end differentiable training pipeline that backpropagates physical execution loss gradients straight through the frozen whole-body controller (SONIC) and Flow-Matching sampler into the VLA action head.

Formulated an effective execution supervision methodology tailored to humanoids, including drift suppression, task transition frame weighting, and coverage-aware sampling to maintain locomotion stability.

sections.heading: Why can't humanoids directly execute motions generated by VLAs?
sections.summary: Unlike fixed arms, humanoids are underactuated systems governed by contact changes and dynamic balance, creating a wide gap between high-level motion intent and low-level physical execution. DiffGR00T bridges this by backpropagating body execution gradients directly into a Flow-Matching VLA via a learned world model.
sections.details:
In robotic arm manipulation, it has been common practice to let low-level servos directly track end-effector poses or joint positions predicted by a VLA. Humanoids, however, are underactuated floating-base systems without fixed feet. They must coordinate walking, manipulation, and posture maintenance while staying balanced, making it extremely difficult for a large VLA model alone to learn high-frequency stabilization control.

Because of this, most existing research adopts a hierarchical architecture: a high-level VLA outputs motion intent (such as latent tokens interpretable by foundation models like SONIC), while a low-level whole-body controller (WBC) consumes proprioceptive feedback to produce joint torques or target positions.

Yet this setup harbors a major pitfall. No matter how hard the controller struggles to stay balanced or how much tracking delay accumulates, those physical execution penalties never propagate back as gradients to the VLA generator. Bridging this via differentiable simulators remains difficult to scale to high-dimensional humanoid full-body control due to foot-contact discontinuities and severe computational bottlenecks.

To solve this, the authors introduced a learned, differentiable world model in place of the simulator. This smooths contact-rich physical transitions into a differentiable formulation, successfully carrying short-horizon execution loss gradients all the way into the VLA action head.

sections.heading: Where Flow-Matching, whole-body control, and differentiable training intersect
sections.summary: Prior Flow-Matching policies and humanoid controllers relied on scalar RL rewards or joint-level residual policies, lacking ways to return physical execution gradients directly to the generator. DiffGR00T is the first framework to stream execution gradients through a token-conditioned controller and sampler using a learned world model.
sections.details:
This study sits at the intersection of three major research areas:

### Flow-Matching Policies and Improvements
Flow-Matching policies, such as $\pi_0$, excel at generating high-quality continuous action chunks. Guidance methods using value functions (like RECAP and Q-VGM) and attempts to differentiate ODE solvers (like VITA) have been proposed. However, none of these directly backpropagate multi-step physical execution losses that pass through whole-body controllers and hardware dynamics.

### Humanoid Whole-Body Behavior Generation and Control
In humanoid loco-manipulation, the standard approach decouples high-level policies from low-level tracking controllers, as seen in SONIC, WholeBodyVLA, and OpenHLM. These frameworks delegate tracking error handling entirely to downstream controllers or residual policies (such as SENTINEL), leaving the high-level generator without a mechanism to be retrained directly on execution outcomes.

### Differentiable Whole-Body Control and Execution-Aware Training
Approaches like DiffMimic differentiate the physical simulator itself, while ControlVAE and SuperMimic optimize policies using learned world models. In particular, SuperMimic trains tracking policies via BPTT over a world model, but no prior work had extended this to large humanoid VLAs equipped with Flow-Matching samplers and frozen whole-body controllers.

sections.heading: How DiffGR00T works: A differentiable loop through the world model and Flow-Matching
sections.summary: DiffGR00T differentiably connects the GR00T N1.7 action head, the frozen SONIC whole-body behavior model, and a learned world model. From a 40-step action chunk, the first 20 steps are executed, and execution losses calculated over a 10-step rollout are backpropagated into the VLA.
sections.details:
The DiffGR00T training pipeline consists of three core components coordinated by a specialized forward and backward pass mechanism:

### Overall Architecture and Control Interface
At deployment (in real-robot or simulator rollouts), only the VLA, the frozen SONIC decoder, and the hand interface are active. The VLA takes images, language, and proprioception, producing a 40-step action chunk via 4-step Flow-Matching Euler integration. Each step consists of a 64-dimensional whole-body motion token and a 14-dimensional hand command. At a 50 Hz control rate, the frozen SONIC decoder $\pi_\psi$ receives the last 10 frames of proprioception history $O_j$ and the motion token $z_j$, outputting a 29-dimensional normalized joint target $u_j$.

### Building the Differentiable World Model
During training only, the physics simulator is replaced by an action-conditioned neural world model $F_\phi$. Rather than predicting absolute states, it predicts state increments $d_t$ at 20 ms intervals, which are integrated to yield the next state $s_{t+1}$. The state vector has 71 dimensions, covering root pose, joint positions, linear and angular velocities, and joint velocities. Training data is compiled from four sources: nominal tracking logs, perturbed token trajectories, closed-loop rollouts, and branched groups testing different tokens from identical initial states. The model is trained once upfront and kept completely frozen thereafter.

### Forward Pass: Imagined Body Execution Rollout
Tokens sampled from the VLA action head pass through a quantization grid via a straight-through estimator (STE) into the frozen SONIC decoder. The resulting joint commands drive the world model through an imagined rollout of $H=10$ steps (0.2 seconds), updating the virtual proprioception history at each step. For the remaining 10 steps, a training-only frozen Critic evaluates the state at step 10 to supply an expected tail return. The execution loss includes root position/orientation drift penalties, joint-limit violation penalties, a 1.5$\times$ weighting on task transition frames, and an anti-stall term to prevent freezing in place.

### Backward Pass: Gradient Flow Through Frozen Modules
From the computed execution loss, gradients propagate backward through time using adjoint variables. They travel through the world model Jacobian $B_i$, the SONIC decoder Jacobian $C_i$, and the 4-step Flow-Matching sampler Jacobians, ultimately updating only the VLA action head (LoRA parameters and output projection layers). The VLM backbone, SONIC, world model, and Critic remain entirely frozen.

sections.heading: Big success rate boosts on simulation benchmarks and real-robot validation
sections.summary: On four HumanoidArena tasks, DiffGR00T boosted the average success rate from 59.2% to 71.7% (+12.5 percentage points) over the supervised baseline and cut steps-to-success by 20%. Closed-loop execution was also demonstrated on the physical Unitree G1.
sections.details:
Experiments were conducted on the Unitree G1 humanoid (29 body DoFs + 14 hand DoFs) within the Isaac Lab-based HumanoidArena environment.

### Benchmark Evaluation (Closed-Loop Performance)
Four tasks were evaluated: OpenDoor, SitSofa, Boxing, and VisionNavi. The authors compared the supervised fine-tuned base VLA (Base) against the DiffGR00T LoRA-updated model (Full).
- Average success rate jumped 12.5 percentage points from 59.2% to 71.7% (OpenDoor: 65.0% $\to$ 78.3%, SitSofa: 48.3% $\to$ 65.0%, Boxing: 71.7% $\to$ 81.7%, VisionNavi: 51.7% $\to$ 61.7%), demonstrating statistically significant gains across all tasks.
- Simulator steps per successful episode dropped roughly 20%, falling from an average of 3,102 to 2,490 steps, with a 30% reduction on SitSofa, which suffered heavily from timeouts. This indicates fewer redundant footsteps, less hesitation, and faster task completion.

### Selecting the Differentiable Horizon $H$
Determining how far into the future the world model can be trusted ($H$) is crucial. Setting criteria of $\ge 70\%$ 4-way ranking accuracy against ground-truth simulation and Kendall's rank correlation $\tau \ge 0.65$, the authors found that $H=5$ was the most accurate (76.8%). However, to provide sufficient credit assignment across the 20-step execution block, $H=10$ (accuracy 70.4%, $\tau=0.67$) was chosen as the longest horizon satisfying the criteria.

### Ablation Studies
Removing individual components highlighted their distinct roles:
- **Coverage-Aware Sampling**: Without it, locomotion stability deteriorated, causing a 3 to 8 percentage point drop across tasks.
- **Transition-Frame Weighting**: Emphasizing pivotal moments like handle contact; removing it caused an approximate 7-point drop on OpenDoor and SitSofa.
- **Anti-Stall Term**: Prevents the robot from freezing; this proved critical for SitSofa, where removing it caused performance to plunge from 65.0% to 50.0%.

### Real-Robot Closed-Loop Validation
Using a physical Unitree G1, closed-loop execution was demonstrated across four behaviors: picking up a trash bag, stepping on a pedal bin to dispose of it, placing a test tube while kneeling, and kicking a soccer ball. This qualitatively confirms that the same differentiable training recipe transfers to real-robot data adaptation.

sections.heading: Current limitations: Coarse surrogate dynamics and unmodeled hands and objects
sections.summary: While the world model provides effective short-horizon gradient signals, it is not an accurate long-term predictor. In addition, 14-DoF hand states and external object dynamics are omitted, and updates are currently strictly offline.
sections.details:
The authors openly acknowledge several limitations:

- **World Model Accuracy**: The learned world model is merely a coarse surrogate for directional gradients, not a substitute for an evaluation simulator. At $H=10$, root position errors reach 3 to 4 cm and orientation errors reach 7 to 8 degrees. Because velocity estimation is notably noisy, its weighting had to be reduced in the loss formulation.
- **Offline Pretraining on Static Data**: The world model is trained once on a fixed dataset without on-policy updates during policy fine-tuning. It cannot fully accommodate distribution shifts as the policy evolves, placing an upper ceiling on potential performance gains.
- **Omission of Hands and Object Dynamics**: Optimization is restricted to the 29 body joints, keeping the 14 hand DoFs fixed to their initial imitation-learned weights. Furthermore, external object states (like doors or sofas) and contact forces are not explicitly modeled within the world model.

sections.heading: Conclusion: A new path forward for execution-aware humanoid VLAs
sections.summary: DiffGR00T achieves differentiable training through a whole-body controller and Flow-Matching sampler using a learned world model. This shifts VLA training from pure token imitation toward genuine physical alignment with the robot's embodied dynamics.
sections.details:
DiffGR00T overcomes the traditional divide where the VLA merely generates intent tokens and the downstream controller blindly tracks them. By introducing a differentiable world model, the framework proves that physical execution penalties deep within the controller can directly guide the Flow-Matching generator head.

In simulation, the approach delivered substantial gains in success rates and execution speed across all four tasks, alongside promising real-robot transfer. Future directions include incorporating object states into the world model, supporting iterative on-policy world model updates, and expanding the optimization to dexterous hands for full whole-body coordination.

takeaways: In humanoid VLAs, the gap between high-level motion token generation and low-level physical execution can be closed via differentiable training with a learned world model.
Without requiring a fully differentiable physics engine, an offline-trained neural dynamics model provides dependable gradient directions over short horizons (~10 steps).
End-to-end backpropagation remains numerically stable even across Flow-Matching samplers (Euler integration) and discrete quantization layers (via STE).
Execution losses require more than simple tracking targets; terms suppressing drift and preventing stalls are crucial for avoiding contact failures and balance loss.
limitations: Coarse world model accuracy leads to noisy velocity estimates, restricting the effective optimization horizon to around 10 steps (0.2 seconds).
The world model is pretrained on fixed offline data, lacking an online update loop to adapt as the policy shifts the state distribution.
The 14 dexterous hand DoFs and external object dynamics/contact forces are omitted from the world model.
